[
1
]

The defendant, Fraser Health Authority, seeks an
order dismissing the entirety of the action brought by Mr. Stephan against
all defendants. The application to dismiss is brought under
Supreme Court
Civil
Rule 9-5 to strike the pleadings, and/or Rule 9-6 for summary
judgment.

Summary of the Claim

[
2
]

The plaintiff’s claim asserts that unidentified
“Jane Does” made false reports to the police and the Ministry of Children and
Family Development (“MCFD”) that the plaintiff sexually assaulted his seven-year-old
daughter (the “Child”). The plaintiff alleges the “Jane Does” are employed by
the defendant, Fraser Health Authority (“Fraser Health”), and states they are
“believed to be nurses and a manager” at the Chilliwack General Hospital (the
“Hospital”). The notice of civil claim (“NOCC” or “the claim”) also alleges
that a different Hospital employee deliberately “set up” the plaintiff to be at
the Hospital for these false reports by neglecting to seek medical care for the
Child.

[
3
]

The plaintiff claims the false reports led to
his daughter being removed from his care for 72 days, and that he suffered
profound “reputational and emotional harm,” specifically public stigma,
nightmares and relapse. The plaintiff seeks to hold Fraser Health vicariously
liable as the employer of the “Jane Does” for his claims in negligence,
defamation, and the intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Grounds for Dismissal

[
4
]

The applicant submits the entire action should
be dismissed:

1.

pursuant to Rule 9-5 as a vexatious abuse of process, because the plaintiff
is attempting to revisit past proceedings and other court orders; and

2.

pursuant to Rules 9-5 and 9-6, because

i)

no duty of care can be owed to the
plaintiff/parent whose child may be in need of protection;

ii)

any reports made by a “Jane Doe” to the MCFD
would have been made under absolute privilege, which is a defence to any tort
claim;

iii)

alternatively, qualified privilege would apply
and there are no material facts to support an allegation of malice on behalf of
the “Jane Does”;

iv)

the defamation claim and intentional infliction
of mental distress fail to plead a reasonable cause of action.

Application to Strike Rule 9-5(1)

[
5
]

At any stage in the proceedings, the Court may
strike the whole or any part of a pleading on the grounds that:

(a)        it discloses
no reasonable claim […],

(b)        it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or

[…]

(d)         it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court …

[
6
]

A claim will be struck if it is plain and
obvious, assuming the facts pled to be true, that the pleading discloses no
reasonable cause of action (
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd
.,
2011 SCC
42
at para.
17
). The test for striking a pleading under Rule 9-5(1)(b) was
summarised in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
at para.
20
:

Under Rule
9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not advance any claim
known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it
would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160 (SC);
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is
pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. …

[
7
]

Abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) is a
flexible doctrine that allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding
where to do so would violate principles of judicial economy, finality and the
integrity of the administration of justice:
Toronto (City) v. Canadian Union
of Public Employees (C.U.P.E.), Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at paras.
35–37
.

Summary Judgment Rule 9-6

[
8
]

On hearing an application brought pursuant to
Rule 9-6 the Court may determine a legal question and pronounce judgment
accordingly, if the Court is satisfied that the only genuine issue is a
question of law.

Application of the Law to this
Claim

[
9
]

The burden is on the applicant to establish that
the claim should be struck or dismissed. I find the applicant has met this
burden for two main reasons: (1) because there is no viable legal pathway for
the claims in negligence to succeed; and (2) because the remaining pleadings do
not give rise to a reasonable claim. I will explain in my reasons below why the
claim in negligence cannot succeed in law. The remainder of the pleadings
allege defamation and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The problem
with these claims is that the facts pled do not provide a sufficient basis to
make out the claims the plaintiff has identified.

[
10
]

The entirety of the plaintiff’s claim must be struck because it
fails to perform the essential function of civil pleadings, that is, to clearly
identify the causes of action being advanced, and to connect each of those actions
with the relevant factual foundations. The plaintiff’s NOCC contains a general
recitation of facts that is either insufficient or too vague to support the causes
of action he advances. The claim does not adequately connect the various facts
alleged to claims against these specific defendants in defamation or the
intentional infliction of emotional distress. In short, the claim as it is
framed does not offer the defendants the required clarity about the case they
have to meet.

[
11
]

However, it is important to recognize that the plaintiff is
self-represented, and his submissions on this application about the relevant
facts amplifies and re-focuses what has been included in the pleadings. In my
view, the live issue on this application is whether the plaintiff should be
granted leave to amend the portions of his claim that do not relate to
negligence. The applicant says such leave should be denied because the entire
action is vexatious and an abuse of process, and because absolute privilege
will ultimately prevent any claim from being successful.

[
12
]

The following questions need to be answered to resolve this
application:

1.         Can a claim in
negligence succeed on the facts alleged?

2.         Do
the facts pled give rise to reasonable claims in defamation and/or the
intentional infliction of mental suffering?

3.         Is
the claim bound to fail due to a defence of absolute privilege?

3.         Are
the claims vexatious or an abuse of the court process?

4.         If
not, should leave be granted to amend the pleadings?

[
13
]

I will consider each of these issues in turn; however first, it is
important to understand the applicable legal framework.

Legal Framework

[
14
]

At the heart of this claim is the fact that the plaintiff’s child
was removed from his care in the course of a child protection investigation by
the MCFD. As I understand the claim, all alleged harms to the plaintiff flow
from this apprehension. The governing legislation for child protection
investigations, including the complaint process is the
Child, Family and
Community Service Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 46 [
CFCSA
].
Section14

of the
CFCSA
creates a positive legal obligation to promptly make a MCFD
report for any person who has reason to believe a child needs protection. The
CFCSA

details a non-exhaustive list of situations in which a child may be in need of
protection, including if they have been emotionally harmed, or sexually
exploited by a parent. A person who fails to report under s. 14 of the
CFCSA

commits an offence (
s. 14(3)
).

[
15
]

In the child protection context, the best interest of the child
takes priority over parental rights (see s. 2 of the
CFCSA
and
Syl
Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. B.D.,
2007 SCC 38
[“Syl Apps”] at paras.
44–45
).
Once a report is made about a child under s. 14, the Director of the MCFD
is obligated to conduct an investigation (
s. 16
,
CFCSA
). The
B.C.
Handbook for Action on Child Abuse and Neglect: For Service Providers
(the
“B.C. Handbook”) clarifies that the legal obligation to report for Fraser
Health service providers arises in the absence of proof or certainty, since it
is the MCFD’s job to investigate, or to determine whether investigation is
warranted. According to the B.C. Handbook, service providers are required to
report any disclosures or indicators they may witness for the MCFD’s
consideration.

[
16
]

There are statutory protections extended to those who make reports
about a child who may be in need of protection, however they are not absolute. Specifically,
s. 101 of the
CFCSA
, which is a statutory ban on legal actions for
damages against a person acting under a duty engaged by the Act, unless they
are acting in bad faith. In addition,
s. 77
of the
CFCSA
mandates
that the Director of the MCFD must refuse to disclose information in a record
that could reasonably be expected to reveal the identity of a person who has
acted on their s. 14 duty to report where the person has not consented to
the disclosure. Public bodies, including the FHA and the RCMP do not have
authority to make such disclosures either (s. 74(2)(e)(i)).

Can a Claim in Negligence Succeed?

[
17
]

It is plain and obvious that there is no claim in negligence against
the Jane Does who allegedly made a child protection complaint to the MCFD. The
applicant has established this aspect of the claim should be struck pursuant to
Rule 9-5(1)(a). I would also strike the claim in negligence as unnecessary, frivolous
or vexatious pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(b) since there is no discernable basis in
law for the claim to succeed. The claim asserts that the Jane Doe defendants
were “negligent in making false reports breaching their duty of care to the
plaintiff to ensure accurate and professional conduct, resulting in foreseeable
harm to the plaintiff and his daughter.” However, the law is clear that no duty
of care is owed to the parent of a child in the child protection context,
whether at an investigative stage or once a child has been found to be in need
of protection: see
Syl Apps
;
C.R. v. Ontario (Child and Youth
Services)
,
2020 ONCA 198
;
C.D. v. Cunningham
,
2014 BCCA 180
and
Quinn
v. British Columbia
,
2018 BCCA 320
.

[
18
]

The reasoning in
Syl Apps
which has been applied to various
different aspects of child protection investigations, hinges on the Supreme
Court of Canada finding a ‘serious and significant’ conflict between parents’
rights and statutory duties that are imposed to promote the best interests,
protection and well-being of children. A proximate relationship between a
plaintiff and defendant is an essential ingredient in any case where a plaintiff
wants to establish that a defendant owes them a duty of care. Claims in
negligence have been struck under Rule 9-5 (or related provisions) because
Courts following
Syl Apps
have relied heavily on public policy reasons in
finding there is no relationship of proximity between plaintiff parents and defendants
who are mandated to protect the plaintiff’s children.

[
19
]

The pleadings in this case do not identify a duty of care owed by
the Jane Doe defendants to the plaintiff, who was not their patient. Given that
the plaintiff submits the Jane Does were not even involved in his Child’s care,
the only apparent legal relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants
is that the plaintiff is the subject of a child protection complaint made by
the defendants. The problem with the plaintiff’s claim in negligence goes
beyond flawed pleadings. In this case, the pleadings are manifestly deficient
in a substantive sense, because there is no proximate relationship between the
plaintiff and the defendants that could give rise to a duty of care (see
E.B.
v. British Columbia (Child, Family and Community Services)
,
2019 BCSC 2200
[
E.B.
]
at paras.
47–49
, 2021 BCCA 47).

[
20
]

In
Syl Apps
, and the cases following it, the defendants were involved
in child protection proceedings either as social workers, their employers, treatment
providers or other professionals who needed to be free to execute their mandate
to treat a child’s interests as paramount without concern for liability to the
child’s family. Similarly to the plaintiffs in
E.B
., the plaintiff here seeks
to distinguish his case from this settled law because the defendants are not
child protection workers or authorities, but rather the complainants who led
the MCFD to become involved.

[
21
]

I accept that people making a child protection complaint may not
have precisely the same statutory obligations to protect children as social
workers or others working in the child protection system. I am also mindful
that finding a duty of care can be a fact driven process, however, any person
who has reason to believe a child is in need of protection, is mandated by

s. 14
of the
CFCSA
to make a report. In this case, the plaintiff
asserts that the complainants were hospital employees who were required to be “accurate
and professional” in relation to the parent of a child who was receiving
treatment at the Hospital.

[
22
]

I find the reasoning in
Syl Apps

continues to apply in the present case, and the plaintiff faces the same
challenges in establishing a proximate relationship between himself and the defendants.
In
B.K. v. Chatham-Kent Children’s Services
,
2016 ONSC 1921
, a similar claim
was brought against a complainant in a child protection investigation. At paras. 52–54
the Court writes:

[52]      In my view, there could scarcely
be a more obvious potential conflict for the person obliged to report suspected
child abuse if he or she also had to consider and balance obligations owed to
the person alleged to have committed the abuse. It is an untenable position. The
legislation has placed a premium on the safety of children, which trumps all
other potential obligations.

[…]

[54]      The
potential conflict of interest in these circumstances negates the imposition of
a duty of care by Dr. Coolbear to the Plaintiffs. Accordingly, the
Plaintiffs’ claim in negligence against Dr. Coolbear must fail. […]

[
23
]

It may be that the applicant is pressing for an expansion of
Syl
Apps
to a factual matrix that has not yet been specifically considered by
appellate Courts, however he has put forward no basis on this application for
the Court to find the defendants owed him a duty of care. Regardless of whether
the claim is bound to fail based on
Syl Apps
, the plaintiff’s claim is manifestly
deficient. The facts pled do not go beyond asserting that the complaint made by
the defendants was false. Whether the complaint made was actually true, or whether
it was capable of raising a child protection issue, is immaterial. The
complaint itself remains part of the child protection investigation. It is the
mandate of child protection authorities to decide what actions to take in the
course of their investigation.

[
24
]

Statutory immunities exist to protect complainants for the sound
policy reasons discussed in
Syl Apps
and its progeny.
Section 101
of the

CFCSA
bars any legal proceeding for damages resulting from the exercise
(or the failure to exercise) any duty under the Act. The only exception to this
statutory bar is where a person acts (or fails to act) in bad faith (s. 101(2)).
This is consistent with
s. 14
of the
Health Authorities Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 180, which applies to any defendants employed by Fraser Health.
This section states there can be no action for damages against any employee for
actions taken ‘in good faith’ in the performance of their duties. Similarly,
privilege and statutory immunities protecting complainants can only be
disturbed where malice is demonstrated.

[
25
]

The plaintiff’s claim makes conclusory statements about a ‘pattern
of malice’ and alludes to a conspiracy between Hospital employees to cause him
harm. The plaintiff argues in submissions that the substance of the complaints
themselves demonstrate that the Jane Doe defendants lacked the necessary “reasonable
belief” that the Child was in need of protection. It is this reasonable belief
that engages the statutory obligation to report, and ensures the complainants
acted in ‘good faith.’ However, none of these facts are asserted in the NOCC. The
case law makes clear that pleadings must disclose the ‘material facts’ to be
relied on in support of a claim. Such facts must go beyond bare assertions and
must have a basis that is more than merely speculative (
Young v. Borzoni
,

2007 BCCA 16
[
Borzoni
] at paras.
25–32
).

[
26
]

I am satisfied that the applicant has established it is plain and
obvious that any claim in negligence will fail. I also find the applicant has
established that the claims in negligence should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b).
Given these insurmountable issues related to the legal basis for a claim in
negligence, leave to amend is denied. The only portions of the plaintiff’s claim
that have any reasonable prospect of success relate to allegations that the
complainants acted maliciously or in bad faith. Having heard the plaintiff’s
submissions, which are much more fulsome than his pleadings, this is where the
heart of his claim appears to lie in any event. The tenor of his oral
submissions is that the defendants had no reasonable belief that the Child was
in need of protection, and they made the report to the MCFD in order to
maliciously cause him harm.

No Reasonable Claim on the Facts

[
27
]

The applicant argues there are several reasons why the claim must be
struck in relation to the remaining causes of action. First, the defence of
privilege would attach to the impugned statements made to authorities. Second,
any claim for damages is statute barred unless there is a basis to find the
defendants were not acting in good faith. Finally, there are factual
deficiencies related to the alleged defamatory statements and in relation to
the damages alleged.

Privilege

[
28
]

The applicant’s primary position is that the report made to child
protection authorities is protected by absolute privilege, since the complaint
was a first necessary step in what ultimately became a court proceeding. In so
doing, the applicant relies on authorities that recognize the long-standing
privilege that attaches to statements made in a court proceeding, and communications
made in the course of inquiry with respect to or in preparation for judicial
proceedings (
Hamouth v. Edwards & Angell,

2005 BCCA 172
at para.
2
).
Absolute privilege would preclude the plaintiff from making any of the claims
alleged, even if bad faith or malicious intention could be established.

[
29
]

However, this kind of absolute privilege only arises where the
statements at issue are made to a quasi-judicial or judicial body. In
Hung v
Gardiner
,
2003 BCCA 257
, the Court adopted the ‘General rule’ for the
application of absolute privilege as follows: “No action will lie for
defamatory statements contained in a document properly used in the course of
any proceedings before a court of justice or tribunal recognized by law.” (
Hung

at para.
6
). Claims in defamation have been struck where the impugned
statements were made to a law society or professional disciplinary colleges. However,
in
Rajkhowa v. Watson
(1998),
1998 CanLII 3273 (NS SC)
, 167 N.S.R. (2d) 108 (S.C.), the Court
declined to find absolute privilege covered a complaint made to the RCMP where
no charges were laid.

[
30
]

Rajkhowa
is discussed by our Court of
Appeal in
Caron v. A
.,
2015 BCCA 47
at paras.
21–24
, with
particular attention to the finding that various steps in a criminal
investigation are not necessarily part of a court proceeding. In
Rjakhowa,

the Court decided “A judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding does not commence
each time the police commence an investigation.” (
Caron
at para.
22
).
The test formulated in
Hung
and endorsed in
Caron
, is “whether
the [recipients of the complaint], exercising their disciplinary powers, have
attributes similar to a court of justice or act in a manner similar to that in
which such courts act.” (
Caron
at para.
24
). The question then, is
not whether the complaint results in litigation, but rather whether the entity
receiving the complaint has a sufficiently judicial quality.

[
31
]

In this case, the plaintiff claims the impugned statements were made
to the police and to the MCFD. There is authority to find that an initiating
complaint to police is not one made to a quasi-judicial or judicial body,
rather as the Court finds in
Rajkhowa
, the police are an investigative
agency. I adopt this reasoning and decline to strike the plaintiff’s claim on
the basis of an absolute privilege defence. In my view, a report made to the MCFD
is akin to an initial police report. I am not persuaded on the materials before
me that the MCFD is an adjudicative body like the law society, medical or
immigration disciplinary colleges as in the cases relied on by the applicant.

[
32
]

I have not been pointed to any provisions in the
CFCSA
that
give the Director the power to adjudicate child protection complaints. Rather,
as the applicant has argued in these proceedings, the MCFD is an investigative
agency. While the Director is empowered and mandated to take action in certain
circumstances, Division 4 of the
CFCSA
makes abundantly clear it is the Provincial
Court that supervises and ultimately adjudicates the legality of the Director’s
investigations and any resulting child apprehensions.

[
33
]

Nor am I persuaded that the circumstances of this case align with
cases such as
Skyllar v. The University of British Columbia,

2022 BCSC
439
at para.
126
, where the alleged defamatory statement was made in the
context of informing settlement negotiations related to litigation between the
plaintiff and the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (“ICBC”). Given the
protections of anonymity in the
CFCSA
, it seems unlikely that the
original complainant in an MCFD investigation would be a witness. Indeed, there
is no suggestion that the complainants in this case played any role in the
court appearances that must have ensued after the Child was apprehended.

[
34
]

The provisions in the
CFCSA
do not provide an absolute
insulation from review, rather, they protect persons performing any duty under
the Act in good faith. The applicant also asserts that any statements made to authorities
are subject to qualified privilege, and that the plaintiff’s claim does not provide
a basis to assert the kind of bad faith or malice that would be capable of
rebutting such a defence. I agree that the claim makes nothing more than a bare
assertion of malice, and must therefore be struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

Malice
or Bad Faith

[
35
]

The legal viability of the plaintiff’s claims in
defamation and the intentional infliction of emotional distress require this
component of malice or bad faith to survive a qualified privilege defence, and
to fall outside the statutory bar on claims for damages created by
s. 101

of the
CFCSA
. As I have outlined already, the NOCC as it stands falls
far short of pleading material facts to support findings of bad faith or malice.
Even though the pleadings say that the originating complaint was untrue,
establishing bad faith requires something more. Simply asserting a ‘pattern of
malice’ is not a material fact. In
Kindylides v. Does,

2020 BCCA 330
at para.
34
,
the Court adopts the following observations of MacDonald J. about material
facts in
Owimar v. Stewart
,
2019 BCSC 1198
:

[19]      … Care must be taken to avoid
undermining the role of pleadings in

identifying the issues by allowing a party
to plead bald assertions or mere

conclusory statements of law. A bald assertion
of a conclusion is not a

pleading of material fact:

[18]      There is
no bright line between material facts and bald

allegations, nor
between pleadings of material facts and the

prohibition on
pleading of evidence. They are points on a continuum,

and it is the
responsibility of a motions judge, looking at the pleadings

as a whole, to
ensure that the pleadings define the issues with

sufficient
precision to make the pre-trial and trial proceedings both

manageable and
fair.

[19]      What
constitutes a material fact is determined in light of the

cause of action
and the damages sought to be recovered. The plaintiff

must plead, in
summary form but with sufficient detail, the constituent

elements of each
cause of action or legal ground raised. The pleading

must tell the
defendant who, when, where, how and what gave rise to

its liability.

Mancuso v. Canada (Minister of National
Health and Welfare),
2015 FCA 227
…

[
36
]

The pleadings in this case do not disclose the full force of what
the plaintiff has alleged in response to this application. In response to the
application to strike, the plaintiff refutes that anything inappropriate
happened at the Hospital. As I understand his position, the plaintiff says the
complainants not only lied about him touching the Child in a sexual manner, but
they acted in bad faith by unreasonably and intentionally complaining about how
the plaintiff handled the Child during the Hospital visits. He suggests they
did so to cause him the foreseeable harm of losing custody of the Child. The
plaintiff submits that when one considers that the young Child was receiving
treatment for a painful abscess in her vagina, it becomes clear that the
complaints about his conduct were intended to prejudice him and not to protect
the Child.

[
37
]

I have taken from the plaintiff’s submissions that when he mentions
a ‘pattern of malice’ in his pleadings, he is referring to the following
constellation of alleged circumstances that he discussed in his response to
this application:

•

the Child’s Mother is the ‘other hospital
employee’ who deliberately set him up for the false accusations to be made;

•

the plaintiff and the Mother are separated and
sharing parenting time of the Child;

•

the Child’s Mother planned the false complaints
to the MCFD because she was embroiled in a legal dispute with the plaintiff
that was scheduled for trial approximately three months after the first false
complaint was made;

•

the Mother did not seek medical attention for
the Child knowing that the plaintiff would have to take the Child to the
hospital during his parenting time to address an abscess in her vagina. This
allowed for the false complaint to child protection authorities, which resulted
in the Child being placed in the Mother’s care;

•

the plaintiff took the Child to the Hospital on
October 24, 2024 and November 23, 2024, to receive treatment for the abscess in
her vagina which included conscious sedation and surgical treatment;

•

the Mother was aware of the Child’s medical
issue before the first Hospital visit. One day before the second Hospital visit,
she left the Child in the plaintiff’s care saying the Child had no medical
problems, when the Child had an obvious issue in her genital area that required
attention;

•

while at the Hospital with the Child, the plaintiff
learned that the Mother worked at the Hospital. He saw her speaking with a
manager and nurses who were not involved in the Child’s care. The plaintiff was
not included in these conversations;

•

the complaints to the MCFD were made after the
October and November Hospital visits by nurses and/or a manager who were not
involved in the Child’s care. The complaints focused on the way the plaintiff
handled the Child while at the Hospital, including putting himself in a
position to see the Child’s genital area when she was receiving treatment,
however this was the area that was receiving medical treatment;

•

the report includes the allegation that the
plaintiff patted the Child’s vagina repeatedly for five minutes while she was on
a stretcher in the ER;

•

the reports were made by Hospital staff who were
not the Mother. The reports were not made by the physicians who treated the
Child, which the plaintiff says supports the inference that the abscess itself
was not indicative of any abuse;

•

the day after the second Hospital visit, the MCFD
apprehended the Child from the plaintiff’s care and the Mother attended court later
that week to obtain an
ex parte
protection order that effectively
deprived the plaintiff of parenting time. The reasons advanced by the Mother at
the protection order hearing included the child’s medical condition and the
fact that she had been removed from the plaintiff’s care by the MCFD;

•

from what is known of the complaints and the medical
file, no physician has opined that the cause of the child’s medical condition
was sexual, however this too was raised at the Mother’s protection order
application;

•

the Mother has a history of deceit and family
violence towards the plaintiff;

•

when police investigated, they found no evidence
of criminal offending by the plaintiff; and,

•

the MCFD then determined there were no
protection concerns with the child being in the plaintiff’s care.

[
38
]

The essential position of the plaintiff appears to be that the complaint
to the MCFD and police was malicious and made in bad faith because it was made
by people with a relationship to the Child’s Mother who had orchestrated an
opportunity to make a false report about the plaintiff to child protection
authorities. The culpability of the Jane Doe defendants centres around their
relationship to the Child’s Mother, who the plaintiff says he is intentionally
not naming as a defendant so as not to elevate conflict between them.

[
39
]

The plaintiff does allude to this joint enterprise in his pleadings by
alleging that the that the Hospital employees (the Jane Doe complainants and
‘the other Hospital employee’) worked together to make the false accusations. However,
the pleadings never say that the ‘other Hospital employee’ is the Mother, nor
does the claim explain a factual basis for asserting the Jane Doe defendants
participated with the Mother in knowingly making misleading allegations to
authorities. Nor do the pleadings reflect the distinctions the plaintiff made
in submissions about the mixture of false and intentionally misleading
allegations he says were made to the MCFD.

[
40
]

The facts that are included in the NOCC are much more limited and untethered
to the specific causes of action that appear to be advanced. The pleadings do
not fulfill their essential function which is to provide the defendants with
the ‘who, when, where, how and what’ gives rise to their liability. Given these
deficiencies in the pleadings, there is no basis to find a reasonable claim
exists and the applicant has established that the remaining claims should be
struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a).

[
41
]

I am mindful in making this decision under Rule 9-5 that there is a
real dispute between the parties with respect to the asserted facts. Whether or
not the complaints made about the plaintiff were maliciously made is very much
in dispute. As such, the Court must be careful not to deprive the plaintiff of
the opportunity for factual determinations to be made at trial. Given that I
will grant the plaintiff leave to amend his pleadings to include a more
expansive recitation of the relevant facts, this is not a suitable time for the
Court to exercise its discretion to grant summary judgment under Rule 9-6. While
it is incumbent on the plaintiff to put their ‘best foot forward’ on such an
application, given the extensive submissions made by this self-represented
plaintiff on the application to strike, I am not convinced this is a situation
where he is simply making vague reference to evidence that may or may not
develop in time. I am prepared to allow the plaintiff the opportunity to fully
and formally advise the Court of the factual basis he relies on before a Court considers
the application to dismiss under Rule 9-6.

Other
Factual Deficiencies

[
42
]

The applicant also points to a heightened requirement in a
defamation claim to particularize the defamatory words spoken. At this point,
the plaintiff has not been provided access to complete information about the
complaint made against him to the MCFD, and so he is in no position to provide
anything more than what he has gleaned through the hearsay contained in the
police reports. In any event, I am not persuaded that the applicant is on firm
ground in submitting the claim should be struck only because the plaintiff relies
on the hearsay in police reports to particularize the defamatory statement.

[
43
]

The passage in
E.B. v. British Columbia
referenced by the
applicant (at paras. 63–66 of the chambers decision) is not determinative.
The Court in
E.B
. did not consider the failure to particularize the
defamation claim independently of the other significant deficiencies in the
pleadings. This is not a situation where the pleadings simply include
unspecified allegations that the plaintiff’s character had been impugned. In
submissions, the plaintiff suggests that the defamatory statements were the
untrue reports of sexual assault made to the MCFD by the Jane Doe complainants.

[
44
]

However, the plaintiff’s position is not clearly expressed in the
NOCC, which alleges defamatory statements that appear to go beyond what the
complainants reported to the MCFD. At para. 11 of the claim, the plaintiff
identifies the specific defamatory statements as ones made verbally and in
writing
by
the MCFD, and not
to
the MCFD by the Jane Doe
defendants. The NOCC does not make clear which statements made by these defendants
are subject to the defamation claim. The claim in defamation must be struck on
this basis.

[
45
]

The applicant also submits that the plaintiff has failed to plead
facts that reasonably support a claim for damages. While the pleadings are not
entirely devoid of facts that could support a claim for damages, establishing
the intentional infliction of emotional distress is a high bar that will
require the plaintiff to produce facts of a provable injury caused by the
flagrant or outrageous conduct of the defendants. The plaintiff’s reliance on
‘relapse and nightmares’ is much too vague and is asserted without a clear
connection to a specific cause of action. As it is currently framed, the
pleadings do not disclose any reasonable claim for damages. The plaintiff also alleges
reputational harm to himself with no clearly articulated connection to defamatory
statements made by these defendants. He also alleges emotional harm to other
family members without explaining the basis on which such harm is compensable.

Is the Claim Vexatious or an Abuse
of Process?

[
46
]

A claim can be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and (d) where the Court
finds it to be vexatious or an abuse of process. An analysis under these Rules
is contextual and the Court will not proceed on the basis that the facts pled
are true. For example, an abuse of process may be made out where the pleadings
are a ‘mere sham’ or the process of the court is being employed for some
deceitful, ulterior or otherwise improper purpose (
Chernen v. Robertson
,

2014 BCSC 1358
at para.
29
). Where the Court finds that the claims offend
these Rules it is unlikely that leave will be granted to amend the pleadings.

[
47
]

The applicant likens the plaintiff’s conduct to cases where a
litigant was found to use the court system “as a plaything to harass others
they do not like.” (
Borzoni
, at para.
64
). The applicant relies on
sound authority that a pleading will be considered vexatious where it causes
the other party anxiety, trouble or expense and is advanced for an improper
purpose such as to harass or to re-litigate settled matters.

[
48
]

The applicant submits the plaintiff’s claim is analogous to the one
considered by the BC Court of Appeal in
Quinn
, where parents commenced
an action against the provincial Crown and representatives of the MCFD after
their children were removed pursuant to the
CFCSA
, only to have the
children returned after four months. The Court decided the claim must be
dismissed as an abuse of process because it was a substantive challenge to the
outcome of the Director’s investigation that should have been resolved within
the framework of the
CFCSA
(at para. 82).

[
49
]

It was significant to the Court’s decision that the parents in
Quinn

did not plead facts in their claim that went beyond those that were available
to them at the presentation hearing when the children were apprehended (at para. 83).
As such, the Court found the parents’ failure to raise those allegations at the
presentation hearing hindered ‘the efficacious operation of the child
protection scheme.’ Raising the allegations years after the apprehension was
found to undermine the child protection litigation even further, and
contributed to the Court’s finding that judicial economy and finality were best
served by striking the claim. In
Quinn
, the BC Court of Appeal not only
dismissed the entire action as an abuse of process, but also dismissed any
application to file an amended claim.

[
50
]

Similarly, in
E.B. v. British Columbia
, a parent sued social
workers and the MCFD in negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, misfeasance and
defamation on the basis that they ‘maliciously misled’ the police to believe
that E.B. was in the process of abducting a child to another country. In this
case, the Court also found an abuse of process on the basis that the claim was
‘an attempt to relitigate the child apprehension process.’ (BCCA decision, at para. 27).
Ultimately the BCCA decided that the chambers judge had found a sufficient
overlap between E.B.’s civil claim and the child protection matter, such that
even if the civil claim was not necessarily a ‘collateral attack’ on the child
protection decisions, the judge could find this to be an ‘informative factor’
in balancing competing interests of judicial economy, consistency and finality.

[
51
]

There are undeniable similarities between the cases relied on by the
applicant and the case at bar. Specifically, at the factual core of the plaintiff’s
claim is his allegation that the defendants acted deceitfully in making a false
complaint to child protection authorities, and that when this complaint was investigated
the Child was removed from the plaintiff’s care for a period of time, only to
be returned a short while later. The harm the plaintiff appears to assert in
his claim is a product of the child protection proceeding, even though it ultimately
concluded with the Child being returned to his care.

[
52
]

However, I also find there are critical differences between the
cases relied on by the applicant and the case at bar. The plaintiff in this
case does not take issue with the MCFD or its investigation, rather, his focus
is on the fact that these authorities were only involved because of what he
claims to be malicious and deceitful information given by the people who planned
or made the originating complaint. Regardless, the grounds warranting apprehension
of the plaintiff’s daughter must have been before the court in the child
protection proceedings where they could have been challenged in that context.
The Courts in
Quinn
and
E.B.
recognize that the reasonableness of
the Director’s grounds to remove a Child are before the court at a presentation
hearing even though it is not ‘
per se
a review or endorsement of the
action that the Director takes.’ (
Quinn
, at para.
82
).

[
53
]

However, unlike the cases cited by the applicant, there is an
absence of evidence before this Court about what transpired at the presentation
hearing, or any of the subsequent child protection proceedings. In
Quinn
,
the Court of Appeal put particular emphasis on the fact that the claim being
struck
did not raise any different facts than those put forward in the child
protection proceedings
. This Court does not have a sufficient evidentiary
basis to make any such finding, and the plaintiff’s submissions suggest that it
was only after the presentation hearing that he discovered further details
about the complaint that triggered the investigation. This significantly erodes
the applicant’s contention that the NOCC is simply a ‘rolling forward’ of other
legal proceedings.

[
54
]

The nature of what the plaintiff is claiming here is separate and distinct
from the conduct of the Director, which is the focus of a presentation hearing.
As the Court in
Quinn
recognizes, the judge at a presentation hearing
does not make findings about whether the child was in fact in need of
protection at the time of removal. “Conflicts in the evidence … are left for
the protection hearing, although the practice is to resolve any conflicts in
the evidence at the presentation hearing in favour of the Director to ensure
the child’s safety …” (at para. 36).

[
55
]

The claim the plaintiff wants to bring appears to differ from the
one in
E.B.
where the Court concluded that “the central thrust of the
plaintiff’s claim is a challenge to the legality of the apprehension of [the
Child].” (at para. 92). The plaintiff here does not contend that the child
protection authorities acted unreasonably, but rather that they acted on
information that had been deliberately intended to mislead their investigation.

[
56
]

I am similarly unable to find that the plaintiff’s reliance on the
ex
parte
protection order is a collateral attack on that order. The
plaintiff’s assertion that harm also flowed from the protection order made
against him is indivisible from the issue he raises about the child protection
complaint. The plaintiff says the protection order was imposed just after MCFD
apprehended the Child, and was vacated just after it was determined no child
protection concerns existed. While it is not made clear in the pleadings, as I
understand it from the plaintiff’s submissions, the significance of the protection
order relates to what the Mother told the Court at the
ex parte
hearing,
not what the Court ultimately decided to do with that information. In other
words, the relevance of the protection order hearing is that, in seeking the
protection order the Mother relied on the results of the complaints to MCFD,
and the Child’s medical condition, suggesting that it was sexually transmitted.

[
57
]

In submitting the claim is vexatious and an abuse of process, the applicant
also says that it is clear from the overall context that the plaintiff is only
bringing this action to harass others and not for any proper legal purpose. I
cannot find that these ulterior motives are made out in this case. The plaintiff
is self-represented. He has marshalled a factual framework (while not in his
pleadings) that at least gives some conceivable basis for an inference to be
drawn that the Mother of the Child intentionally used the child protection
investigation to deprive the plaintiff of parenting time.

[
58
]

The defendant Jane Does are only culpable on the plaintiff’s version
of events to the extent that they acted on an animus that the Mother harboured
against the plaintiff. It is not the Court’s role on an application such as
this to engage in a fine-tuned weighing of the strength of this evidence,
however there must be more than bare assertions of conspiracy and wrongdoing
for the claim to advance.

[
59
]

When it comes to the involvement of the Jane Does, the plaintiff
suggests there are factual inferences available to the Court as a result of the
relationship between the Jane Does and Mother. He relies on the fact that they all
work at the Hospital together, and that the fact that he saw the Mother and the
people he believes to be the Jane Does conferencing with one another while the
Child was being treated. The plaintiff also points to the fact that the Jane
Does were not directly involved in the Child’s care, and that the MCFD and
police determined in relatively short order that the Child was not in need of
protection. The plaintiff emphasizes that he is constrained in making any more
detailed allegations, particularly about the relationship between the Mother
and the defendants because of the confidentiality protections that shield him
from discovering the identities of the complainants.

[
60
]

The plaintiff submits this Court should allow the pleadings to
survive through to the disclosure phase of litigation, and not foreclose the
possibility of a viable action prematurely (
Thmbran v. The British Columbia
College of Nurses and Midwives (BCCNM)
,
2024 BCSC 441
). For the reasons I
have already given, the NOCC must be stuck because fundamental facts about the
plaintiff’s allegations of bad faith, defamation and damages are not included
in the pleadings. However, the Court must go on to consider whether leave should
be granted to amend. The Courts take a liberal approach to permitting the
parties to amend pleadings and will generally only refuse to do so where it is
plain and obvious the amendment is bound to fail
(
E.B.
at para.
84
).
A finding that the claim is an abuse of process or vexatious would be strong
reasons to deny such leave.

[
61
]

While it remains to be seen whether the plaintiff is able to frame
his claim such that there is more than a mere speculative basis on which the
Court could find the defendants liable, given the constellation of evidence
about acrimonious family proceedings between the plaintiff and the Mother, the
apparent relationship between the Mother and the complainants, and the unsubstantiated
complaints made to the MCFD, I am not prepared to strike the pleadings without
allowing the plaintiff to amend them. The plaintiff should also be permitted to
clarify his pleadings regarding the defamatory statements and damages
generally.

[
62
]

The applicant submits that allowing leave to amend will only
perpetuate a vexatious attempt to harass Hospital employees. The applicant
relies heavily in making this argument on the plaintiff’s tenacity in pursuing
the identities of Hospital employees he believes actually made the child
protection complaint against him. However, given the facts that he alleges, and
in particular the importance of understanding any relationship between the
Mother and the staff she was seen consulting with during the Hospital visit,
his efforts do not appear to be without reason.

[
63
]

The plaintiff says he learned from police that the complainants were
Hospital employees who were not the Mother, and who were not involved in the
Child’s care. The plaintiff has been directed by various authorities to seek
their identities through proper channels so that he can name the Jane Doe’s in
his claim. I cannot find in the circumstances that his conduct is vexatious and
abusive. The circumstances fall short of establishing the applicant’s theory
that the plaintiff has commenced this action simply to harass Hospital
administrators or employees. As the plaintiff points out, the way this action
was framed was in part a response to direction he received at a previous court
appearance to add the unknown defendants to the action.

[
64
]

The crux of the plaintiff’s claim is that he wants someone held
accountable for the harm that flowed to him from what he says was an
intentional decision to mislead child protection authorities about what
happened when he brought his daughter to the Hospital for medical treatment. The
Court in the
CFCSA
proceedings is not likely to have engaged with the
truthfulness of the allegations against him at the presentation hearing. The plaintiff
submits it is a legitimate use of the court process to allege that the
originating complaint was an intentional fraud.

[
65
]

Having considered all of these factors, I cannot find the applicant
has established that the claim should be struck under Rule 9-5(1)(b) or (d).

Conclusion

[
66
]

It is plain and obvious that the plaintiff’s claim in negligence must
fail for the legal reasons I have outlined above. The claim in negligence is
struck, without leave to amend and is dismissed. While the pleadings do not
clearly explain the factual basis for negligence, the evidence and submissions
provided by the plaintiff suggest the Jane Does were negligent in making a
wrongful child protection report, and that Fraser Health is vicariously liable.
Given that there can be no cause of action in negligence in such circumstances,
this aspect of the pleadings must be struck against all defendants.

[
67
]

The absence of facts supporting the conclusory assertion that the complaint
to the MCFD was made in bad faith precludes the advancement of any other part
of this action. The pleadings are also struck pursuant to s. 9-5(1)(a) in
relation to the balance of the claim. For any torts to constitute a reasonable
claim, there must be a basis in the facts to find the defendants acted in bad
faith or with a malicious intent to harm the plaintiff. This is not clearly set
out in the pleadings. The allegations of harm in the pleadings are also too
vague to reasonably support a claim for damages, and the defamatory statements
identified in the claim do not appear to be attributed to the Jane Doe
defendants. However, given the constellation of evidence referred to by the
plaintiff in response to this application, I am satisfied that he should be
granted leave to amend his pleadings.

[
68
]

The information available to the plaintiff about the MCFD report has
evolved. He has expressed a desire to seek legal advice, which he would be well
advised to do. I am mindful that the broader factual matrix asserted at the
application to strike does not fit easily into his claim for the intentional
infliction of emotional distress. While the plaintiff has relied on
J.P. v.
British Columbia (Children and Family Development),

2017 BCCA 308
, he does
not plead misfeasance, which is a tort that captures conduct specifically
intended to injure a person.

[
69
]

The plaintiff’s NOCC is not one that can be brought into compliance
with the
Rules
by simply striking specific portions. The entire claim
will be struck and I encourage the plaintiff to seek legal advice if he will be
amending the claim to conform with the
Rules
. I am granting leave for a
fresh claim to be filed. In so doing, I am giving significant weight to the
fact that Mr. Stephan is self-represented, and this will be the first time
he has been granted leave to amend his pleadings.

[
70
]

While I am granting leave to amend with respect to any claim other
than negligence, I am mindful that the plaintiff has not furnished the Court or
the defendants with his proposed amendments. Given the plaintiff is
self-represented, I will put him on notice that if he finds himself before the
Court on another application to strike, he should come prepared with proposed
amendments, if that is what he is seeking.

[
71
]

I decline to make any ruling with respect to the disclosure orders
the plaintiff seeks in his NOCC. These claims are best considered if and when
the plaintiff assembles a viable amended claim.

[
72
]

Finally, the applicant is entitled to costs since they have been
substantially successful on this application. Costs are awarded in the
defendants’ favour, and will be determined on the ordinary scale.

“Ormiston J.”
